data.why: A Roman stone arch bridge over a creek that runs toward the camera. Each fix is built part by part: a plank, a slab, then a stone arch on a wooden frame. The camera starts on the plank, stays on the bridge side-on, and ends on a wide shot of the finished bridge with a cart crossing.

ideas.idea: a plank across a creek is the simplest bridge there is
stone is stronger than wood, so build two piers and lay a slab across
a loaded cart rolls onto the plank and it snaps in the middle
stone does not like to bend, so the long slab cracks in the middle
a wooden frame holds wedge stones in a curve until the keystone locks them
the finished curve with a road on top is a Roman arch
each stone presses on the next, so weight turns into squeeze, which stone handles best
the arch pushes sideways at its feet and tries to spread apart
heavy stone piled at both ends holds the feet in place
cement is not what holds the arch up; the stones stand dry on their own weight
stone walls along the edges and a cart rolling safely across
a calm bridge with a cart crossing, built from nothing but stone, weight and a curve

chain.shows: a loaded cart rolls onto the plank and the plank snaps in two, tipping the cart toward the water
chain.stakes: the cart and its load fall into the creek

chain.shows: a dark crack opens in the middle of the long stone slab
chain.stakes: anyone crossing, and the whole slab

chain.shows: the two feet of the arch slide outward and the crown opens
chain.stakes: the whole bridge could fall into the creek

surprises.claim: Stone is roughly ten times stronger when squeezed than when stretched
surprises.search: granite compressive strength vs tensile strength ratio
